Maintenance records and technician assessments determined that the stoppage was caused by the overspeed governor tripping on the upward run combined with a worn door interlock contact on the third-floor landing door. Normal operations resumed the next day at 8:05 a.m. after power was restored and the safety circuit was reset.

Finishing floor supervisor Imogen Pask responded to the third-floor landing to communicate with Bram and subsequently transferred the remaining fabric bolts to the third floor using stairs and the small passenger lift. Bram exited the car unhurt after remaining trapped for approximately 25 to 40 minutes, and the unit was tagged out of service until the following morning. Maintenance records and technician assessments determined that the stoppage was caused by the overspeed governor tripping on the upward run combined with a worn door interlock contact on the third-floor landing door. Normal operations resumed the next day at 8:05 a.m. after power was restored and the safety circuit was reset.

On a Tuesday in early March around 05:40, freight train 7114 consisting of two locomotives and 26 cars derailed on the Osterby curve of the Kestrel Branch. Shortly before the incident, a wayside detector recorded the train passing at 38 miles per hour with no overheated axle bearings. As the train approached the curve, the signal displayed a clear aspect, but the engineer felt a sudden lurch through the cab floor and applied the emergency brake. The dispatcher immediately halted all traffic on the branch and called the maintenance office. Seven cars ended up off the rails, with three lying on their sides, causing bundles of timber to slide down the embankment and several bags of fertilizer to split open. Two crew members walked away from the wreck, and one was treated for a bruised shoulder at the scene by an ambulance crew that arrived 19 minutes after being called. Maintenance crews cleared the cars using two heavy cranes, shoveled the spilled fertilizer into containers, and replaced about 90 meters of track before the line reopened.

On October twenty-second, an incident occurred at the Vessel Hythe Land Registry at approximately half past one in the morning following six hours of heavy rain. A rooftop cooling tank holding roughly twelve thousand litres overflowed, sending water into the basement server room. Basement water sensors had started detecting moisture near the east wall at one thirty-six, and a flood alarm soon reached the guard console. Night security guard Ines Okafor heard running water and noticed corridor emergency lighting while on ground floor rounds. Upon opening the basement door, she observed water about four centimetres deep spreading across the floor. Because the nightly backup finished just before one, no title records were lost, and only the two lowest rack-mounted storage units were touched by standing water as levels peaked. An engine crew arrived with a portable pump and departed at three-fifty. Public counters remained closed all the following morning.

On a Tuesday in early March around 05:40, freight train 7114 consisting of two locomotives and twenty-six cars derailed on the Osterby curve of the Kestrel Branch. Shortly before the curve, a wayside detector recorded the train passing at thirty-eight miles per hour with no overheated axle bearings. On October twenty-second, an incident occurred at the Vessel Hythe Land Registry at approximately half past one in the morning following six hours of heavy rain. A rooftop cooling tank holding roughly twelve thousand litres overflowed, sending water into the basement server room. Basement water sensors had started detecting moisture near the east wall at one thirty-six, and a flood alarm soon reached the guard console. Night security guard Ines Okafor heard running water and noticed corridor emergency lighting while on ground floor rounds. Upon opening the basement door, she observed water about four centimetres deep spreading across the floor. The sump pump started shortly before two in the morning but experienced a high-level fault, causing it to run at reduced output. Okafor contacted registry IT systems lead Tomas Brandl and called the Hythe Fire Service. Brandl performed a remote database shutdown from home. Because the nightly backup finished just before one, no title records were lost, and only the two lowest rack-mounted storage units were touched by standing water as levels peaked. An engine crew arrived with a portable pump and departed at three-fifty. Public counters remained closed all the following morning.

Sources: Registry Facilities Incident Report, Sump Pump Controller Log, Night security guard Ines Okafor, Registry IT Systems Lead Tomas Brandl, Hythe Fire Service Call Record, Basement Water Sensor Array

On a Tuesday in early March around 05:40, freight train 7114 consisting of two locomotives and twenty-six cars derailed on the Osterby curve of the Kestrel Branch. Earlier that night, the dome shutter had been closed at 00:50 due to incoming snow, and site records show the generator had last undergone a routine test run 11 days prior to the storm. When the generator halted, control room lighting failed and the dome drive lost power, although the battery-backed computers remained operational. Visiting astronomer Dr. Odalys Renk, stationed in the visitor wing preparing data, observed that corridor lights went dark as the generator noise faded. Site engineer Talwen Pryce, residing in the nearby staff cottage 300 metres away, traversed the snow on foot in approximately ten minutes, manually reset the lockout at the generator panel, and successfully restarted the unit at 02:04. Data from the fuel tank level gauge record indicated the tank was 61 percent full at 01:00 and 48 percent full at 02:00, confirming the absence of any sudden fuel drops between 01:00 and 02:10.
